questions.question: A 17-year-old develops abrupt severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea and vomiting. What is the safest immediate FNP action?
choices: Schedule routine outpatient ultrasound next week
Treat empirically for a UTI and reassess tomorrow
Arrange immediate emergency evaluation for possible testicular torsion
Reassure because adolescents commonly have benign pain
questions.explanation: Sudden severe unilateral scrotal/testicular pain, especially with nausea/vomiting, is an acute-scrotum pattern. Testicular torsion is time-sensitive and requires immediate emergency evaluation; do not delay for routine outpatient testing.

questions.question: Which symptom is classified primarily as a voiding lower urinary tract symptom?
choices: Urgency
Nocturia
Weak urinary stream
Urge incontinence
questions.explanation: Weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, and straining are voiding symptoms. Urgency, frequency, nocturia, and urge incontinence are storage symptoms.

questions.question: A patient with chronic weak stream now cannot void, has painful suprapubic fullness, fever, and malaise. Which interpretation is safest?
choices: This is routine BPH and can wait for a follow-up in several weeks
This may be acute retention with infection/obstruction and needs urgent or emergency evaluation
The fever proves the problem is only a viral illness
Overflow leakage rules out retention
questions.explanation: Inability to void with painful distention and systemic symptoms raises concern for acute retention, obstruction, and infection. The patient needs prompt assessment rather than a delayed chronic-LUTS plan.

questions.question: Which statement about hematuria in a patient taking an anticoagulant is most accurate?
choices: The medication proves that no further evaluation is needed
Anticoagulation may contribute to bleeding but does not exclude an underlying urinary-tract lesion
Hematuria is always caused by infection
Only microscopic hematuria needs follow-up
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation can increase visible bleeding but should not be used to dismiss infection, stone disease, renal disease, or malignancy. Evaluate the clinical pattern and ensure closed-loop follow-up.

questions.question: A patient reports a new painless firm testicular lump that has persisted for two weeks. What is the best next principle?
choices: Assume it is benign if pain is absent
Provide timely diagnostic imaging and an appropriate urology/specialty pathway
Wait until it becomes painful before testing
Treat with antibiotics without examination
questions.explanation: A painless testicular lump or persistent change requires timely evaluation. Benign conditions can mimic malignancy, so reassurance alone or delay is unsafe.

questions.question: Why should erectile dysfunction be assessed as more than an isolated sexual symptom?
choices: It always has a single psychological cause
It can reflect vascular, metabolic, neurologic, hormonal, medication, mental-health, or relationship factors
It is an inevitable part of aging and needs no review
It excludes cardiovascular disease
questions.explanation: ED commonly has multifactorial causes and can be a useful entry point to review cardiometabolic risk, medications, mood, sleep, neurologic disease, and patient goals.

questions.question: What is the appropriate approach to a digital rectal examination when it is clinically indicated?
choices: Perform it without explanation because it is routine
Explain the purpose, obtain consent, protect privacy, offer a chaperone according to policy, and respect a patient’s choice to decline
Use it as the only prostate-cancer test
Avoid documenting limitations if it is declined
questions.explanation: Genitourinary examinations are consent-based. A DRE can add selected information but is not a stand-alone cancer test, and an incomplete examination must be documented with an alternate plan when needed.

questions.question: What is the best role of post-void residual (PVR) measurement in a patient with LUTS?
choices: It independently diagnoses BPH
It helps assess incomplete emptying or retention in the appropriate clinical context
It replaces history and urinalysis
A normal PVR excludes all urinary disease
questions.explanation: PVR can help establish whether incomplete emptying or retention is present and can guide further evaluation. It does not by itself establish the cause or exclude other conditions.

questions.question: Which presentation most strongly supports emergency rather than routine outpatient disposition for hematuria?
choices: One remote self-limited episode with a documented benign cause
Gross hematuria with clots, inability to void, severe pain, fever/obstruction, anemia symptoms, or unstable vital signs
A normal prior cancer screening test
A patient who has no urinary symptoms today
questions.explanation: Gross hematuria with clot retention, obstruction, systemic illness, significant bleeding, or instability can require urgent stabilization and evaluation. Prior screening does not supersede acute physiology.

questions.question: Which element is essential to a safe outpatient plan for a stable men’s-health complaint?
choices: Tell the patient to return only if they feel worried
Document the diagnostic question, result/referral owner, follow-up access, and specific emergency return precautions
Avoid discussing barriers to specialty care
Assume a single negative test ends the diagnostic process
questions.explanation: Symptoms can evolve and tests can be incomplete. A safe plan specifies who owns results and referrals, when follow-up occurs, and which changes—such as inability to void, severe pain, fever, fainting, heavy bleeding, or worsening symptoms—require immediate care.
